releases.title: Two Plead Guilty to Unemployment Insurance Benefits Fraud Conspiracy
releases.teaser: SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Las Vegas residents Ricky Lee Ware, 43, and Kimberly Ann Wallace, 30, pleaded guilty today to conspiracy to commit access device fraud, U.S. Attorney Eric Grant announced. According to court documents, between July 2020 and January 2021, the defendants conspired to obtain debit cards that allowed them to access unemployment benefits. The unemployment benefits were in the names of people who did not know the defendants. The defendants then used the debit cards to withdraw more than $900,000 in unemployment benefits from ATMs. Ware and Wallace are scheduled to be sentenced by U.S. District Judge Dena Coggins on Feb. 19, 2027, and face a maximum of 7.5 years in prison. The third defendant in the case, Carlos Lee Sanchez Jr., 46, of Sacramento, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit access device fraud in June 2026 and is scheduled to be sentenced Nov. 13, 2026. This effort is part of a California COVID-19 Fraud Enforcement Strike Force operation.

releases.title: Justice Department Charges 28 Foreign Nationals in California for Election Crimes
releases.teaser: Federal law enforcement throughout California today arrested 11 foreign nationals living in the United States who are among 28 total charged in criminal complaints with federal crimes, including that they fraudulently registered to vote in U.S. elections, electoral contests in which most of them cast illegal and fraudulently obtained ballots. Today’s arrests are part of “Operation Protect the Vote” – a coordinated effort among all four California-based United States Attorney’s Offices to combat and root out fraud in U.S. elections and protect electoral integrity. All 28 foreign nationals charged are lawful permanent residents (LPRs), or “green card” holders. Although LPRs have legal immigration status in the United States, they are not U.S. citizens and are not permitted to vote in U.S. elections. The criminal charges include making false statements in a naturalization application and some of the defendants also are charged with fraudulent voter registration. Both charges are felonies that carry a maximum penalty of five years in federal prison. Broken down by jurisdiction, the following defendants are charged in today’s takedown: Central District of California All the following defendants below in this jurisdiction face felony charges, including false statements in a naturalization application: Omar Alexander Muñoz, 72, a Belizean national living in Commerce, California, fraudulently registered to vote in September 2019, claiming his was a U.S. citizen, then voted in U.S. elections in 2020, twice in 2022, and in 2024. He also lied on his application to become a naturalized U.S. citizen when he falsely stated under oath to have never claimed to be a U.S. citizen. Amandeep Kaur, 30, an Indian national living in Rancho Palos Verdes, California, and who is seeking to become a U.S. citizen, fraudulently registered to vote in December 2022 and voted in the November 2024 U.S. election. Ana Domínguez, 60, a Salvadoran national living in Long Beach, California, fraudulently registered to vote in July 2006 and lied in her naturalization paperwork in March 2026. Axel Giovani Prera García, 46, a Guatemalan national and Pico Rivera, California, resident, fraudulently registered to vote in 2002 and 2005, and lied in his naturalization paperwork in June 2025. Flavio Alejandro Zúñiga, 43, a Mexico national and La Puente, California, resident, fraudulently registered to vote in 2003 and lied in his naturalization paperwork in February 2026. Butleng Taing, 43, a Cambodian national living in Long Beach, fraudulently registered to vote in July 2021, voted in the 2022 and 2024 U.S. elections, and lied on his naturalization paperwork in August 2025. Carlos Antonio Galeas, 54, a Honduran national and West Covina, California, resident, fraudulently registered to vote in 2012 and 2016, then lied in his naturalization paperwork in September 2018. Ernest Gutiérrez Ruvalcaba, 57, a Mexican national living in Wilmington, California, fraudulently registered to vote in February 2024 and voted one month later. Jesús Narez-Madrigal, 52, a Mexican national living in Carson, California, fraudulently registered to vote in 2014, voted in the 2024 U.S. general election, and lied in his naturalization paperwork in June 2024. José Antonio Bañuelos-Díaz, 42, a Mexican national and West Adams, California, resident, fraudulently registered to vote in 2007 and lied on his naturalization paperwork in March 2025. Rouzbeh Seyamaknejad, 63, a Canadian national and Rancho Palos Verdes, California, resident, fraudulently registered to vote in December 2018, lied in his naturalization application in January 2024, and voted in the November 2024 U.S. election. Eastern District of California The following defendants are charged with voting by an alien in a federal election, a misdemeanor that carries a statutory maximum sentence of one year in federal prison: Maricela Nazarín González, 43, a Mexican national living in Clovis, California, registered to vote in 2020, indicating that she was a U.S. citizen, and voted in elections in 2022, twice in 2024, and 2025. Rony de Jesús Sicaja, 38, a Guatemalan national living in Fresno, California, fraudulently registered to vote in 2017, and voted in the June 2022 primary election and the November 2024 general election in the United States. Camino Giles Jiménez, 51, a Mexican national living in Kerman, California, knowingly voted in three U.S. elections despite knowing he is a noncitizen, the most recent election being the June 2026 primary. Juan Antonio Rivas García, 46, a Mexican national and Sacramento, California, resident, fraudulently registered to vote in 2018 and 2020, both times falsely asserting under oath that he was a U.S. citizen. Rivas voted in the 2022 and 2024 U.S. elections. Giezell Viduya Adawag, 41, a Philippines national and Vacaville, California, resident, fraudulently registered to vote the day of the November 2024 general election, falsely certified that she was a U.S. citizen, and voted in the election that day. He is charged via information. Northern District of California The following defendants are charged with attempted procurement of naturalization contrary to law, false statement under oath in any matter relating to naturalization or citizenship, and voting by an alien: Verónica Bullene, 43, a.k.a. “Verónica Hernández Martínez,” a Mexican national living in Petaluma, California, made false statements on her naturalization application that she had never claimed to be a U.S. citizen when, in fact, she did so under penalty of perjury to register to vote in 2022 and 2023 then voted in 2024. releases.title: Former Employee of State of Illinois Subcontractor Indicted for Allegedly Fraudulently Obtaining More Than $4.6 Million in Covid-Relief Benefits
releases.teaser: ANDREA WELLINGTON engaged in fraud related to the Pandemic Unemployment Assistance (“PUA”) program, one of the sources of relief under the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (“CARES”) Act, according to an indictment returned in U.S. District Court in Chicago. Wellington worked as a customer service representative for a company that subcontracted with the Illinois Department of Employment Security (“IDES”). The position gave her access to the IDES PUA system, the indictment states. IDES determined the amount of each payment to be issued to PUA claimants based, in part, on the amount of income that the claimant had earned prior to the filing of their claim for PUA benefits. The more wages reported, the greater the amount of the PUA payment. The charges allege that in the fall of 2021, after Wellington had been terminated from her position with the IDES subcontractor, she and co-defendant RANDALL EASLEY accessed the IDES PUA system and fraudulently increased the wage histories of hundreds of PUA applicants, causing IDES to disburse approximately $4,680,582 in PUA payments to which the recipients were not entitled. The indictment alleges that Wellington and Easley modified the wage histories in exchange for thousands of dollars from the applicants. Wellington, 35, of Chicago, is charged with 21 counts of wire fraud, while Easley, 38, of Chicago, is charged with 14 counts of wire fraud. Wellington and Easley were arraigned in federal court on Oct. 8, 2026, and pleaded not guilty to the charges.

releases.title: Two Florida defendants sentenced to prison for nearly $900,000 health care scam
releases.teaser: According to court documents, the following defendants pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit health care fraud, mail fraud, and wire fraud: Steven Anthony Churchill, 39, of Boca Raton, Florida, was sentenced to 24 months in prison; Samson Kollelil Solomon, 28, of Pompano Beach, Florida, was sentenced to 24 months in prison; and Fawn Lickteig, 46, of Lawrence, Kansas, will be sentenced on November 10, 2026. In March 2020, Steven Churchill bought Free State Pharmacy (FSP) in Lawrence, Kansas, but under the name of a now deceased, accused coconspirator. FSP operated as a mail-order pharmacy despite representing itself to Medicare as a retail pharmacy.

releases.title: Muncie Man Accused of Falsely Requesting over $1 Million in COVID-19 Relief Tax Credits
releases.teaser: Gregory Vernon Dupree, 38, of Muncie, has been charged in a federal indictment with eight counts of filing false COVID-19 claims,including claims for the Employee Retention Credit (ERC) and COVID‑related Sick and Family Leave credits. These charges were brought as part of the Trump Administration’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud. According to the indictment, between January 2021 and January 2022, Dupree allegedly filed eight Forms 941 (Employer’s Quarterly Federal Tax Return) with the Internal Revenue Service. Through these filings, Dupree made claims against the United States requesting refunds totaling over $1 million, knowing those claims to be false.

releases.title: Waipahu Women Sentenced to Two Years in Prison for Pandemic and Tax Fraud While Earning Millions from an Unlicensed Construction Business
releases.teaser: Heidi Cafirma, 46, of Waipahu, Hawaii, was sentenced on September 30, 2026, by United States District Judge Shanlyn A.S. Park to 24 months in prison followed by 3 years of supervised release for filing false tax returns and wire fraud. Cafirma was also ordered to forfeit $70,500 and pay up to over $1 million in restitution, which total amount will be determined by the court at a later date. Cafirma pled guilty pursuant to a plea agreement in December 2025. In 2020, the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act created the Pandemic Unemployment Assistance (PUA) unemployment insurance program to provide emergency unemployment payments to certain workers whose livelihoods were impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic but who were ineligible for traditional state unemployment insurance benefits, such as business owners, self-employed workers, independent contractors, and those with a limited work history who were out of business or had significantly reduced their services as a direct result of the pandemic. To obtain either traditional unemployment insurance (UI) or PUA UI benefit payments, claimants could submit a claim online. If approved, the U.S. Treasury typically deposited payments every week into a claimant’s bank account. To continue to receive benefit payments, claimants were required to certify on a weekly basis under penalty of law that they remained unemployed or partially employed, and eligible to receive benefit payments. According to court documents, Cafirma admitted that between June 2020 and September 2021, she submitted 22 false claims online for UI benefit payments for herself by repeatedly falsely certifying under penalty of law that she was unemployed and not receiving income, despite knowing that her certifications were false because she received over $1 million in income during that period from her and her husband’s unlicensed construction business. Cafirma fraudulently obtained at least $70,500 in unemployment insurance and PUA UI benefits to which she was not entitled.

releases.title: New Haven Man Pleads Guilty to Pandemic Relief Program Fraud Offense
releases.teaser: DAVANTE MALLARD, 33, of New Haven, waived his right to be indicted and pleaded guilty today before U.S. District Judge Sarah F. Russell in New Haven to an offense stemming from a pandemic relief program fraud scheme. According to court documents and statements made in court, in March 2020, Congress passed legislation that sought to mitigate the economic harm caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Legislation included the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act (the CARES Act), which created employee retention credits (ERCs) that were intended to repay employers for certain costs expended to retain employees during the pandemic and permitted businesses to recoup previously paid wages and certain health insurance costs, and the Families First Coronavirus Response Act, which created the sick and family leave credit (SFLC) that reimbursed small and mid-sized employers for the cost of providing paid sick and family leave wages to employees for leave related to COVID-19 during the pandemic. Mallard owned Mallard Dynasty Realty Group (MDR Group), which provided real estate and property management services. The business earned little to no income, had no employees, had not paid wages, and had not filed W-2 forms with the Internal Revenue Service. In early 2022, Mallard was contacted by individuals who he knew who instructed him to open an online account with a business that provided online tax preparation services. Mallard than provided the individuals with the account information and password. Between April 2022 and February 2023, the individuals accessed the account and prepared and filed with the IRS fraudulent Employer’s Quarterly Federal Tax Returns (Forms 941) for MDR Group. The Forms 941 misrepresented the number of employees and total wages paid, and were used to apply for large ERC and SFLC refunds. When contacted by the IRS to verify information about MDR Group, Mallard provided false information, including that his business had five employees. Between August 2022 and March 2023, MDR Group received from the IRS six refund checks totaling $256,906. Mallard kicked a portion of the refund monies back to the individuals who orchestrated the scheme. Mallard pleaded guilty to making false claims regarding IRS refunds, an offense that carries a maximum term of imprisonment of five years.

releases.title: Slidell Man Sentenced for Cares Act Fraud
releases.teaser: MARCEL GROSS (“GROSS”) , age 56, of Slidell, was sentenced on October 13, 2026 by U.S. District Judge Darrel James Papillion, to four years’ probation and the payment of $350,272 in restitution, for conspiracy to commit wire fraud, announced U.S. Attorney David I. Courcelle. GROSS fraudulently obtained a Paycheck Protection Program loan, which was a form of assistance authorized by the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

releases.title: National Fraud Enforcement Division Obtains Guilty Plea of Pensacola Postal Worker for PPP Loan Fraud
releases.teaser: Dominique J. Stanberry, 33, of Pensacola, Florida, pleaded guilty in federal court to two counts of wire fraud involving Small Business Administration (SBA) Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan funds. This prosecution was part of the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud launched by President Donald J. Trump, a whole-of-government effort to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The plea was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida. U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “We saw unprecedented levels of fraud during the COVID-19 pandemic by scammers, like this defendant, who sought to enrich themselves by ripping off the American taxpayer, but my office will tirelessly pursue those fraudsters to make them pay for their crimes. Anyone in the Northern District of Florida who abuses or defrauds a Federal benefit program should be on notice: my office is coming for you.” Court documents reflect that in 2021, the defendant, while working full time as a United States Postal Service employee, caused to be submitted a fraudulent online application for a PPP loan that falsely claimed she was self-employed with a business that lost income due to the COVID-19 pandemic. As a result of her fraud, the defendant received $20,833 in PPP loan funds to which she was not entitled.

releases.title: Sanford Woman Sentenced for Theft of Government Money
releases.teaser: U.S. District Judge John A. Woodcock, Jr., sentenced Cori Godin , 47, to 18 months in prison, to be followed by three years of supervised release. Godin was also ordered to pay $37,105 in restitution. Godin pleaded guilty on November 18, 2025. According to court records, Godin falsely claimed to be unemployed in order to receive unemployment insurance benefits, including federally funded benefits intended to address the COVID-19 pandemic. Unemployment insurance is a joint state and federal program that provides monetary benefits to eligible beneficiaries. Payments are intended to provide temporary financial assistance to lawful workers who are unemployed through no fault of their own. Beginning in about March 2020, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, several federal programs expanded unemployment insurance eligibility and benefits. For a period of approximately 13 months in 2020 and 2021, Godin falsely claimed to be unemployed and received approximately $37,105 in benefits.

releases.title: Texas residents charged with promoting Illegal tax shelter
releases.teaser: a federal grand jury in Dallas, Texas returned an indictment on Sept. 22, 2026, charging four Texas residents with conspiracy to defraud the United States and other crimes for promoting an illegal tax shelter. According to the indictment, Texas residents Duncan John MacDonald, Sarah Duren, Richard Ronald Cayce and Thomas Weickgenant promoted and sold a fraudulent trust scheme that was used to shelter more than $1.5 billion of income, causing an estimated tax loss to the IRS of more than $200 million.

releases.title: Somerset Lifesciences Inc. Agrees to Pay $4M to Resolve Allegations of Causing Medicare to Pay Claims for its Mislabeled Generic Drug
releases.teaser: Somerset Lifesciences Inc. (Somerset) has agreed to pay $4 million to resolve common law claims for causing Medicare Part D (Medicare) to pay for its prescription-only (Rx-only) generic drug Olopatadine when it was no longer eligible for Medicare coverage. Medicare does not cover drugs that can be purchased by retail customers over-the-counter (OTC) without a prescription. In 2020, the brand name version of Olopatadine switched from Rx-only to OTC, and Somerset was required to change Olopatadine’s label from Rx-only to OTC as well. Instead, Somerset continued to label and sell Olopatadine as Rx-only and caused Medicare to wrongfully pay claims for an OTC drug.
releases.stage: Civil settlement (allegations only, no determination of liability)

releases.title: Negril Agrees to Settle Allegations of Improper Medicaid Billing
releases.teaser: To resolve allegations that Negril Incorporated and its owners violated the False Claims Act and the Virginia Fraud Against Taxpayers Act by causing false claims to be submitted to the Virginia Medicaid Program, the company has agreed to a $1,817,910.60 civil settlement. The Government alleged that, from January 2021 through May 2022, Negril billed Virginia Medicaid for certain mental health skill‑building services under its National Provider Identification (NPI) number. However, the company that actually provided those services to Virginia Medicaid beneficiaries did not have its own NPI, was not credentialed through the Virginia Department of Behavioral Health and Developmental Services and was not enrolled as a Medicaid provider. Under the parties’ billing arrangement, Negril submitted the claims to Virginia Medicaid, remitted 75 percent of the Medicaid reimbursement to the other company, and retained the remaining 25 percent.
releases.stage: Civil settlement (no admission of wrongdoing, no determination of liability)

releases.title: Dover Contractor and Owners Pay $295,204 to Settle Postal Service Overbilling Claims
releases.teaser: Garrett Mechanical Inc., a Dover repair and maintenance contractor; Hey Brother, LLC, a Florida limited liability company; Joseph Bruni; and Daniel Tulchin have agreed to pay $295,204 to resolve allegations that they violated the False Claims Act by overbilling the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) for work performed at Postal facilities. Garrett Mechanical Inc., owned and operated by Bruni, began providing repair and maintenance services at USPS facilities in February 2021. In May 2022, Hey Brother, owned by Tulchin, purchased substantially all of Garrett Mechanical Inc.’s assets. Following the sale, Bruni continued to work for Hey Brother, which did business as Garrett Mechanical, and reported to Tulchin. The companies performed work for USPS until September 2023 and billed USPS approximately $263,576 between 2021 and 2023. As part of the settlement, the defendants admitted that from February 2021 through September 2023, the companies submitted claims to USPS that included inflated labor hours, inflated material costs, false completion certificates, and forged signatures of USPS employees. As a result, USPS paid the companies more than it owed under the service agreement.

releases.title: Wyoming County Business Owner Pleads Guilty to Immigration Fraud
releases.teaser: Peggy Jill Hendrick, 58, of Pineville, pleaded guilty today to fraud and misuse of visas, permits, and other documents. Hendrick admitted that she falsified employee eligibility verification forms for seven illegal aliens who worked at her restaurant. According to court documents and statements made in court, on February 18, 2026, a law enforcement officer inspected the Pineville restaurant owned by Hendrick to check if every employee had a Form I-9, Employment Eligibility Verification. As part of her guilty plea, Hendrick admitted that she falsely told the officer that she possessed a completed I-9 form for each employee. The officer told Hendrick that she had three business days to produce the I-9 forms for review. Hendrick admitted that following the inspection, she prepared I-9 forms for seven employees she believed were highly likely illegal aliens and not authorized to work in the United States.

releases.title: Massachusetts Man Charged for His Role in Marriage and Immigration Document Fraud
releases.teaser: A federal grand jury returned an indictment charging Jingming Chen, 31, of Quincy, Massachusetts, with Conspiracy to Commit Marriage Fraud and Immigration Document Fraud. According to allegations in the indictment, Chen, a U.S. citizen, was paid by a Chinese national co-conspirator residing in Aurora, Ohio, to enter into a sham marriage and commit immigration document fraud by fabricating evidence to support the false claim that their marriage was legitimate. They submitted false statements to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Service (USCIS) to obtain lawful permanent resident status—commonly known as a Green Card—and other immigration benefits for the co-conspirator.

releases.title: ICE HSI Arrests Non-Citizen for Illegally Voting in 2024 Election
releases.teaser: Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) arrested Mukeshkumar Somabhai Chaudhari, a non-citizen, for knowingly making a false claim of United States citizenship to vote in the 2024 general election. On September 10, a federal grand jury in the District of Minnesota returned the two-count indictment charging Chaudhari with allegedly making the false citizenship claim. According to the indictment, on or about November 5, 2024, Chaudhari signed the voter signature certificate required by Minnesota law to vote in the general election. The certificate required him to swear or affirm that he was a citizen of the United States. The indictment alleges Chaudhari was not a U.S. citizen and knowingly made the false citizenship statement in order to vote.

releases.title: DOL OIG Great Lakes Region Announces Charges and Arrests in Multiple Unemployment Insurance Fraud Schemes Tied to Gang Activity
releases.teaser: DETROIT — On October 6, 2026, Derrick Thompson, a multi-convicted felon with previous charges of fraud, assault and felony firearms violations, was arrested by DOL-OIG and ATF agents for his role in an unemployment insurance (UI) fraud scheme. Thompson was previously charged with one count of bank fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft. He is alleged to have filed dozens of UI claims in his own name and in the names of others not associated with him, defrauding various state workforce agencies (SWA) of approximately $400,000 in UI benefits.

releases.title: Two defendants charged in superseding indictment alleging $19 million health care fraud scheme targeting federal workers’ compensation program

According to the indictment, from 2017 to 2023, the defendants engaged in a scheme to submit false and fraudulent claims to the U.S. Department of Labor’s Office of Workers’ Compensation Programs (OWCP). FECA provides medical and wage benefits to federal employees injured on the job. In total, the conspirators submitted roughly $19 million in fraudulent claims, resulting in at least $17 million in payments from the FECA program. The indictment alleges that the defendants and their coconspirators each received a share of the proceeds. Jabeen and Brown were both arrested and had their initial appearances on Oct. 14. If convicted, the defendants each face a maximum sentence of 10 years’ imprisonment.

Yesterday, Akinade Adedeji Raheem, 43, of Nigeria, was arraigned on a federal indictment and detained in the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service pending further proceedings. releases.title: Two Aliens From Sudan and Afghanistan Charged for Illegal Voting
releases.teaser: LAS VEGAS – Today, two aliens, one from Sudan and one from Afghanistan, have been charged for illegally voting in a federal election in Nevada. Yousif and Safi are each charged with one count of voting by an alien. The maximum statutory penalty is one year of imprisonment, a fine of up to $100,000, or both. releases.title: Justice Department Charges 18 More in North Carolina with Illegally Voting in 2024 Election
releases.teaser: Today, the Justice Department announced that 18 aliens, including an illegal alien, in North Carolina have been indicted for illegally voting. Nine were charged in the Eastern District of North Carolina, five were charged in the Middle District of North Carolina, and four were charged in the Western District of North Carolina. These indictments are in addition to 12 individuals who were previously indicted in the Eastern District of North Carolina for illegally voting, bringing the statewide total to 30 indicted this year. “Illegal voting is just that: illegal,” said Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter. “If you’re not an American citizen, you cannot vote in our federal elections. We want to prevent illegal voting from occurring, which is why we’ve now charged 30 people just in North Carolina who have violated our laws by illegally registering to vote and illegally voting. We need to preserve the integrity of the ballot box by ensuring only those eligible are casting ballots.” “Protecting the integrity of our elections is fundamental to preserving our constitutional republic,” said U.S. Attorney Ellis Boyle for the Eastern District of North Carolina. “Indeed, the right to vote is the primary seed from which all other rights and liberties sprout. When noncitizens steal your vote, they can create an unamerican government that strips all liberty and freedom from citizens. Every unlawful ballot silences the voice of a lawful voter, striking at the core of our great nation. This is not a victimless crime; every citizen who casts a lawful vote is a victim. You do not know which citizen’s lawful vote that illegal vote cancelled out, so it cancels out every lawful vote. With these nine indictments, added to the 10 we announced earlier this month and two from earlier in the year, we make it crystal clear: we will not tolerate illegal voting in North Carolina. Let these 21 indictments serve as an unmistakable message ahead of the 2026 election: if you vote illegally, we are looking, we will find out, and we will prosecute you.” “The right to vote is fundamental to American citizenship and a cornerstone of our republic,” said U.S. Attorney Dan Bishop for the Middle District of North Carolina. “This office is committed to protecting the integrity of our elections and ensuring that laws enacted to ensure fairness and secure our rights are upheld. These charges serve notice that those who violate our election laws, including non-citizens who register and vote, will be investigated and prosecuted.” “In our most recent elections in North Carolina — the 2025 municipal elections — there were 14 races decided by 2 votes; 15 races decided by 1 vote; and 7 races that were tied ,” said U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson for the Western District of North Carolina. “Every vote matters. And the public must have confidence that our elections are conducted fairly and that every ballot cast is a lawful one.” “The integrity of federal elections is essential to the health of our democracy,” said Special Agent in Charge Reid Davis of the FBI Charlotte Field Office. “Every FBI field office assigns dedicated election‑crimes coordinators because protecting the election process is core to our mission. When questions about voter eligibility arise, we work closely with our state and federal partners to review records, confirm the facts, and ensure election laws are honored. Any violation erodes public trust and dilutes valid votes. When any aspect of our democratic process is threatened, the FBI will act decisively to defend it.” “The integrity of our electoral system depends on rules that are applied consistently and enforced without fear or favor,” said Special Agent in Charge Mark M. Zito of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Carolinas. “HSI’s role is clear: We investigate complex threats to the homeland, including fraud that undermines public trust in vital national systems. We will continue to work with our partners to protect the public’s confidence in America’s electoral system.” Eastern District of North Carolina A federal grand jury has indicted nine more noncitizens, including an illegal alien, for illegally voting in the 2024 election. These indictments build on the 12 indictments U.S. Attorney Boyle unveiled on Oct. 15, including another illegal alien, for illegally voting in the 2024 North Carolina elections, bringing the total to 21 individuals indicted in the Eastern District of North Carolina for illegally voting. The most recent indictments allege that all nine defendants falsely claimed to be U.S. citizens to register and vote in the 2024 general election. These charges reflect the Department of Justice’s commitment to protecting the integrity of federal elections and ensuring that only eligible U.S. citizens participate in them. The grand jury returned indictments against the following aliens: Selvin Porfidio Gonzalez Escobar, 43, an illegal alien from Guatemala living in Robeson County, North Carolina, is charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. He registered to vote in 2020 and voted in the 2024 and 2020 general elections. Amerigo Di Nolfi, 53, a native of Italy, citizen of the United Kingdom, and lawful permanent resident of the United States now residing in Hampden County, Massachusetts, is charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. He registered to vote in 2024 and voted in the 2024 general election in New Hanover County, North Carolina. Elizabeth Margaret Crudup, 52, a native of Kenya and a lawful permanent resident residing in Harnett County, North Carolina is charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. She registered to vote in 2008 and voted in nine general elections in 2024, 2022, 2020, 2018, 2016, 2014, 2012, 2010, and 2008, as well as nine Primary Elections in 2026, 2024, 2022, 2020, 2018, 2016, 2014, 2010, and 2008. Gregory Eugene Wade, 64, a native of Bermuda and a lawful permanent resident residing in Wake County, North Carolina, is charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. He registered to vote in 2000 and voted in 12 general elections in 2024, 2022, 2020, 2018, 2016, 2014, 2012, 2010, 2008, 2004, 2002, and 2000, as well as the 2020 and 2002 primary elections. Jacqueline Yvonne Papandreou Brown, 63, a native of Singapore, citizen of the United Kingdom, and lawful permanent resident of the United States residing in Duplin County, North Carolina, is charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. She registered to vote in 2020 and voted in the 2024 general election. Karl Anthony Wilkins, 62, a native of Jamaica and a lawful permanent resident now residing in Fulton County, Georgia, is charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. He registered to vote in 2018 and voted in the 2024, 2022, and 2020 General Elections, as well as the 2020 primary election in Wake County, North Carolina. Patricia Elena Valencia Cardona, 56, a native of Colombia and a lawful permanent resident residing in Harnett County, North Carolina, is charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. She registered to vote in 2024 and voted in the 2024 general election. Richard John Reid, 62, a native of the United Kingdom and a lawful permanent resident residing in New Hanover County, North Carolina, is charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. He registered to vote in 2002 and voted in four general elections in 2024, 2020, 2012, and 2008 general elections, as well as the 2012 and 2008 primary elections. Taso Gretes, 58, a native of Greece, a citizen of Canada, and lawful permanent resident of the United States residing in New Hanover County, North Carolina, is charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. He registered to vote in 2022 and voted in the 2024 general election. Middle District of North Carolina Five individuals have been charged with illegal voting and, in some instances, unlawfully claiming U.S. citizenship, in connection with the 2024 election in the Middle District of North Carolina. Adrianus Marinus Van Der Staak, a Netherlands national and a lawful permanent resident of the United States living in Seagrove, North Carolina, is charged by indictment with one count of knowingly making a false statement or claim of U.S. citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. Saida Adali Hirachete Olivarez, a Mexican national and a lawful permanent resident of the United States living in Reidsville, North Carolina, is charged by indictment with one count of knowingly making a false statement or claim of U.S. citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. Juan Florencio Ramos, a citizen of Cuba and lawful permanent resident of the United States living in Salisbury, North Carolina, is charged by indictment with one count of knowingly making a false statement or claim of U.S. citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. Phillip Alexander Carter, a native of Barbados and a lawful permanent resident of the United States living in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, is charged by indictment with one count of knowingly making a false statement or claim of U.S. citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. Yamila Avalos, an Argentinian national and a lawful permanent resident of the United States living in Concord, North Carolina, is charged by information with one count of voting by an alien. Western District of North Carolina Four aliens have been indicted for illegally voting in federal elections in the Western District of North Carolina. A federal grand jury in Charlotte returned criminal indictments charging the following individuals: Michael Agah, 74, a Nigerian national and lawful permanent resident of the United States residing in Charlotte, is charged with voting by an alien and making a false claim to U.S. citizenship to vote. The indictment alleges that Agah falsely stated and claimed that he was a U.S. citizen on an Authorization to Vote Form. Then on Nov. 5, 2024, Agah voted in a federal election. Luis Alberto DeJesus, 50, a Dominican national and lawful permanent resident of the United States residing in Conover, North Carolina, is charged with voting by an alien in a federal election and making a false claim to U.S. citizenship to vote. It is alleged that DeJesus falsely stated on an Early Voting Application that he was a U.S. citizen and thereafter voted on Oct. 30, 2024, knowing that he was not a U.S. citizen and was not legally permitted to cast a ballot. Serge Christian Dupont, 57,a French national and lawful permanent resident of the United States residing in Charlotte, is charged with voting by an alien and making a false claim to U.S. citizenship to vote. It is alleged that on Nov. 5, 2024, Dupont made a false statement and claimed that he was a citizen of the United States on an Authorization to Vote Form. Dupont then did vote on the same day in a federal election. A fourth individual has been charged by a criminal bill of information.Edread Ray Stanley, 63, a national of St. Kitts and Nevis and a lawful permanent resident of the United States residing in Charlotte, is charged with voting by an alien. It is alleged that Stanley, knowing that he was not a U.S. citizen, knowingly voted on Nov. 5, 2024, in a federal election. Additional Details The charges of falsely stating or claiming U.S. citizenship to vote carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. Voting by an alien carries a maximum penalty of one year in prison and a $100,000 fine. Upon conviction, a federal district court judge will determine any imposed sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. FBI and HSI are investigating the above cases. The U.S. Attorney’s Offices for the Eastern, Middle, and Western Districts of North Carolina are prosecuting the cases in their respective districts. An indictment or information merely contain accusations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
